Ajloun_Castle_English_Long.story:
Welcome to Ajloun Castle!  
The stone fortress sits atop one of the mountains of Ajloun Governorate in northern Jordan. It was built in 1184 by ʿAz‑d‑Din Osama, a commander of Saladin. The castle was erected to protect northern Jordan and to watch the trade routes linking the Levant with the Jordan Valley. Its strategic position offers wide views of the surrounding hills and valleys. Inside you will see defensive towers, stone passages, living quarters and storage rooms. The builders also created wells and rain‑water tanks to keep life going during a siege. Over the centuries the Mamluks added expansions and new parts. Parts of the structure suffered damage from earthquakes, but later restorations repaired them. Ajloun Castle was part of a network of Islamic forts that defended the region in the Middle Ages and played an important role in resisting the Crusader campaigns. Today the castle is surrounded by the beautiful Ajloun forests and stands as one of Jordan’s most prominent historic and tourist landmarks.  
Take your time and explore every stone.

Ajloun_Castle_Français_Long.story:
Bienvenue au château d'Ajloun !  

Perché sur l’une des montagnes de la province d’Ajloun, au nord de la Jordanie, le château s’élève depuis 1184 m, construit par le chef musulman — Az‑d‑Dîn Osama, l’un des commandants de Saladin. Sa position stratégique offre une vue étendue sur les montagnes et les vallées environnantes, idéale pour surveiller les routes commerciales entre le Levant et la vallée du Jourdain.  

Les murs abritent des tours défensives, des passages de pierre, des chambres d’habitation et des entrepôts de provisions. Entouré des forêts d’Ajloun, parmi les plus belles zones naturelles de Jordanie, le site est aujourd’hui l’un des monuments historiques et touristiques les plus remarquables du royaume.

Al_Maghtas_English_Medium.story: Welcome to Bethany Beyond the Jordan! This sacred site lies east of the Jordan River, north of the Dead Sea. The area includes Tel al‑Kharrar, also called the hill of the prophet Elijah. Baptismal pools and water channels used in religious rites were found on the ground. Al_Maghtas_English_Long.story: Welcome to Bethany Beyond the Jordan! This site lies east of the Jordan River, north of the Dead Sea, and is known as Bethany Beyond the Jordan. Christians believe it is where John the Baptist baptized Jesus. Archaeological digs since 1996 have uncovered churches, monasteries and baptismal pools from the Roman and Byzantine periods. The area includes the hill of Kharrar, also called the hill of the prophet Elijah or Mar Elias. Baptismal pools and water channels used in religious rites were found here. During the Byzantine era the site was an important Christian pilgrimage center. Floods and earthquakes damaged the structures, leading to multiple reconstructions over the centuries. After the 1994 Jordan‑Israel peace treaty, mines were cleared, the site was rediscovered and restored. UNESCO listed the baptismal site as a World Heritage site in 2015 for its global religious and historical value. Thousands of pilgrims and tourists visit each year, especially on the Feast of the Baptizer when Christians commemorate Jesus’ baptism. Take a moment to feel the history beneath your feet and explore this remarkable place.

Al_Maghtas_Français_Medium.story:
Bienvenue à Béthanie au‑delà du Jourdain !  
Vous vous tenez à l’est du fleuve Jourdain, au nord de la mer Morte, sur le site appelé Beth Anya en Jordanie. Selon la tradition chrétienne, c’est ici que Jean le Baptiste a immergé le Seigneur Jésus. Depuis 1996, les fouilles ont mis au jour des églises, des monastères et des bassins baptismaux datant des ères romaine et byzantine. Le mont Kharrar, aussi nommé la colline du prophète Élie, domine le paysage. On y a découvert des bassins dédiés au baptême et des canaux d’eau employés lors des rites. Le lieu était un centre de pèlerinage chrétien à l’époque byzantine. Des inondations et des séismes ont entraîné plusieurs reconstructions. Après le traité de paix de 1994, les mines ont été retirées, le site a été redécouvert et restauré. L’UNESCO l’a inscrit au patrimoine mondial en 2015, reconnaissant sa valeur religieuse et historique. Chaque année, des milliers de pèlerins et de touristes viennent, surtout lors de la fête du Baptême.  
Continuez votre découverte de ce lieu exceptionnel.

Al_Maghtas_Français_Long.story:
Bienvenue à Béthanie au‑delà du Jourdain !  

Imaginez‑vous debout sur le site du « Moghtas », à l’est du fleuve Jourdain, au nord de la mer Morte, connu sous le nom de Bethanie à travers la Jordanie. Selon la tradition chrétienne, c’est ici que Jean le Baptiste aurait baptisé le Seigneur Jésus. Depuis 1996, les fouilles ont mis au jour des églises, des monastères et des bassins baptismaux datant des périodes romaine et byzantine. Le mont Kharrar, aussi appelé la colline du prophète Élie ou Mar Elias, domine le paysage. Des bassins dédiés au baptême et des canaux d’eau, employés dans les rites religieux, ont été découverts sur place.  

Durant l’ère byzantine, le Moghtas était un centre de pèlerinage chrétien important. Le site a subi des inondations et des séismes, ce qui a entraîné plusieurs reconstructions au fil des siècles. Après le traité de paix jordanien‑israélien de 1994, les mines ont été retirées, le site a été redécouvert et restauré. En 2015, l’UNESCO l’a inscrit sur la liste du patrimoine mondial pour sa valeur religieuse et historique. Chaque année, des milliers de pèlerins et de touristes affluent, surtout lors de la fête du Baptême, pour commémorer le baptême du Christ.  

Continuez votre exploration et laissez‑vous imprégner par la magie du lieu.

Surrounded by the Jordan Mountains to the east, it offers stunning sunset views. Explore and enjoy this unique place.

Dead_Sea_English_Medium.story: Welcome to the Lowest Point on Earth! The Dead Sea lies between Jordan and Palestine and is one of the region’s most famous natural landmarks. It is the lowest point on the planet, more than 430 meters below sea level. Its water is extremely salty, about ten times the salinity of ordinary seas, so its density lets visitors float easily without swimming. The black mud is rich in natural minerals used for skin care, and the water contains magnesium, potassium and calcium with therapeutic benefits. Surrounded by the Jordanian mountains to the east, the view is especially beautiful at sunset. No fish or large marine life live here because of the high salt, which gave the sea its name. Come and experience this unique place for yourself.

Dead_Sea_English_Long.story: Welcome to the Lowest Point on Earth! The Dead Sea lies between Jordan and Palestine and is one of the most famous natural landmarks in the region. It is the lowest point on the planet, dropping more than 430 meters below sea level. Its water is extremely salty, about ten times the salinity of ordinary seas, which makes the water so dense that visitors float easily without swimming. The black mud is rich in natural minerals and is used for skin treatment and care. The water contains minerals such as magnesium, potassium and calcium that have therapeutic benefits. The site is a major tourist and spa destination in Jordan, welcoming guests from around the world. Mountains of Jordan rise on the east side, offering stunning scenery especially at sunset. No fish or large marine creatures live there because of the high salt level, which is why it is called the Dead Sea. Its natural resources have been used for medicine and beauty since ancient civilizations. Feel the unique atmosphere and explore this remarkable place.

Dead_Sea_العربية_Long.story:
أهلًا بك في أخفض بقعة على وجه الأرض! أمامك موقع يمتد بين الأردن وفلسطين، وهو من أشهر المعالم الطبيعية في المنطقة. هنا تنخفض السطح إلى أكثر من 430 مترًا تحت مستوى البحر، ما يجعله أخفض نقطة على الأرض. مياهه شديدة الملوحة، تصل إلى عشرة أضعاف ملوحة البحار العادية، لذا فإن كثافتها العالية تسمح لك بالطفو بسهولة دون الحاجة إلى السباحة. 

الطين الأسود الذي يغطي القاع غني بالمعادن الطبيعية، وتحتوي مياهه على مغنيسيوم وبوتاسيوم وكالسيوم، وهي معادن يُستفاد منها في العلاج والعناية بالبشرة. لهذا السبب يُعد الموقع وجهة سياحية واستشفائية بارزة، يستقبل زوارًا من جميع أنحاء العالم. 

من الشرق تحيط به جبال الأردن، فتُضيف منظرًا خلّابًا خاصة عند غروب الشمس. لا توجد أسماك أو كائنات بحرية كبيرة هنا بسبب ارتفاع الملوحة، وهذا هو سبب تسميته. منذ آلاف السنين استُخدمت موارده في الطب والتجميل، وكان معروفًا لدى الحضارات القديمة. 

استمتع بالمنظر، جرب الطفو، واكتشف فوائد المعادن؛ ثم واصل استكشاف هذا المكان الفريد.

Dead_Sea_Français_Long.story:
Bienvenue au point le plus bas de la Terre !  

Imaginez le paysage où le Jordan et la Palestine se rejoignent, où s’étend le célèbre Mer Morte, la plus basse surface de notre planète, plus de 430 m sous le niveau de la mer. L’air porte une odeur saline, et l’eau, dix fois plus salée que les mers ordinaires, possède une densité telle que chaque pas vous fait flotter sans effort, comme si vous étiez porté par un coussin invisible.  

Le sable noir qui tapisse le rivage cache une boue riche en minéraux – magnésium, potassium, calcium – que les civilisations anciennes utilisaient déjà pour leurs soins et leurs remèdes. Aujourd’hui, les visiteurs du monde entier viennent ici non seulement pour la sensation unique de flotter, mais aussi pour profiter de ces propriétés thérapeutiques et de beauté.  

À l’est, les montagnes jordaniennes encadrent le lac, offrant des panoramas spectaculaires, surtout lorsque le soleil se couche et colore le ciel. Aucun poisson ne survit dans ces eaux hyper-salées, d’où le nom qui rappelle son caractère exceptionnel.  

Le Mer Morte reste une destination touristique et de bien‑être majeure en Jordanie, un lieu où la nature, la santé et la beauté se rencontrent. Continuez votre exploration, le spectacle ne fait que commencer.

Jerash_English_Long.story: Welcome to the City of a Thousand Columns! Jerash lies in northern Jordan, about 48 kilometers from Amman. It is one of the best preserved Roman cities in the world, with origins that reach back to ancient times and a flourishing during the Greek and Roman periods. Known as Gerasa, it was a member of the Decapolis league. As you walk, the famous oval forum opens before you, one of the most beautiful Roman squares worldwide. The Street of Columns links the main sights, its massive stone columns guiding your steps. You will pass two Roman theatres, the southern and the northern, and you can see important temples such as the Temple of Artemis and the Temple of Zeus. Although several earthquakes have damaged some buildings, large parts remain intact, showing layers of Greek, Roman, Byzantine and Islamic influence. Every year the Jerash Festival of Culture and Arts draws visitors from around the globe. Today Jerash stands as one of Jordan’s most important tourist and archaeological sites. Take your time and explore the marvels around you.

Karak_Castle_English_Long.story: Welcome to Karak Castle! The fortress sits in the city of Karak, south Jordan, about 120 kilometers from Amman. Its construction began in 1139 and finished in 1142 during the Crusader period. Built on a high rocky outcrop, the walls follow the irregular shape of the stone. Deep dry ditches protect the north and south sides, and a bridge over the ditch leads to a broken entrance that is hard for attackers to breach. Inside, an upper courtyard holds a church, olive and grape presses, bakeries, and a Mamluk palace. Below, subterranean halls and rooms now house a museum displaying artifacts from Karak Governorate. Crusader builders used gray‑pink stone, while later Ayyubid and Mamluk additions employed limestone. Saladin reclaimed the castle after his 1187 victory at Hattin, and the Ayyubids and Mamluks later reinforced it. Today the castle stands as one of the largest and most important historic forts in Jordan, bearing the layers of Crusader, Ayyubid and Mamluk civilizations. Take your time and explore every stone.

Karak_Castle_Français_Long.story: Bienvenue au château de Kerak ! Imaginez-vous sur le promontoire rocheux qui domine la ville de Kerak, à environ 120 kilomètres au sud d’Amman. Petra_English_Long.story: Welcome to the Rose City! Petra lies in Ma'an Governorate in southern Jordan. The Nabataeans founded it over two thousand years ago and made it their capital. It flourished as a trade hub linking Arabia with the Levant and Egypt. The city is famous for its buildings carved directly into pink stone, which is why it is called the Rose City. The Siq serves as the main entrance, a narrow rocky passage that leads visitors to the Treasury, the most photographed monument with a precisely carved façade. Inside the site you will also find the Monastery, the Nabataean theater, the colonnaded street and royal tombs. The Nabataeans developed an advanced engineering system to collect and store rainwater, helping them live in the desert environment. Petra became part of the Roman Empire in 106 AD. It was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1985 and chosen as one of the New Seven Wonders in 2007. Today it remains one of Jordan’s and the world’s top archaeological tourism destinations. Enjoy exploring this remarkable place.

Qasr_Amra_English_Long.story: Welcome to Qasr Amra! This desert palace sits in the eastern Jordanian desert, about 85 kilometers east of Amman. It was built in the early eighth century during the Umayyad era and is attributed to Caliph al‑Walid ibn Yazid. The Umayyads used it as a royal retreat, a hunting lodge and a place for leisure. Inside you will find a reception hall and a complete Umayyad bath, one of the oldest Islamic baths. The walls are covered with colorful frescoes, some of the finest examples of early Islamic art. The paintings show scenes of hunting, daily life, kings, stars and constellations. Above the bathing chamber, the ceiling bears an astronomical panel, among the oldest preserved sky drawings in the Islamic world. The palace is a striking example of Umayyad architecture in a desert setting. Um_AL_Jimal_English_Long.story: Welcome to the Black Oasis! Umm Al‑Jimal lies in Mafraq Governorate, north Jordan, about 86 kilometres from Amman. It is called the Black Oasis because its buildings are made of black basalt stone. The site began as a Nabataean settlement and later flourished in the Roman and Byzantine periods. It served as an important stop on ancient trade routes that linked the Arabian Peninsula with the Levant. Today more than 150 archaeological structures remain, including houses, churches and towers. The town was known for an advanced system that collected rainwater and stored it in ponds, wells and tanks. During the Byzantine era it grew into a religious centre with many churches. It stayed inhabited through the Umayyad period until a large earthquake in 749 AD caused its decline. The ruins show the succession of Nabataean, Roman, Byzantine and Umayyad cultures in one place. In 2024 UNESCO added Umm Al‑Jimal to the World Heritage List for its historical and cultural value. Take your time and explore this remarkable place.

Les habitants avaient mis au point un système avancé de collecte des eaux de pluie, stockées dans des bassins, puits et citernes. Sous la domination byzantine, le site se transforma en un centre religieux avec de nombreuses églises. Il resta occupé pendant l’ère omeyyade, jusqu’au tremblement de terre dévastateur de 749 ap. J‑C., qui provoqua son déclin.  

Les ruines d’Umm al‑Jimal illustrent la succession des civilisations nabatéenne, romaine, byzantine et omeyyade en un seul lieu. Inscrite au patrimoine mondial de l’UNESCO en 2024, elle continue d’attirer les curieux.

Um_Qais_English_Long.story:
Welcome to Umm Qays, where the ancient city of Gadara meets nature and breathtaking panoramic views.  

Umm Qays sits in Irbid Governorate, northern Jordan, about 28 kilometers from Irbid city. Perched on a high plateau, it looks over the Jordan Valley, the Yarmouk River, Lake Tiberias and the Golan heights. In antiquity the place was called Gadara, one of the Decapolis cities, and it flourished as a centre of culture, art and poetry.  

The ruins are famous for black basalt stone used in many structures. You will see a western theatre built of that basalt, a street of columns, the Decumanus Maximus, Roman baths, a nymphaeum, the “Path of the Nymphs”, markets and warehouses. Byzantine‑era churches and other buildings show the Christian presence.  

Inside the Ottoman house known as Beit al‑Rousan, now the Umm Qays Archaeological Museum, are statues, mosaics, pottery, sarcophagi and architectural fragments. A memorial inscription by the poet Arabius speaks of life’s fleeting nature.  

Nearby, the hot springs of Al‑Hamma have been valued for their healing properties since ancient times.  

Umm Qays has passed through Greek, Roman, Byzantine, Islamic, Ottoman and modern phases, and it was chosen from 136 villages for the 2022 Best Tourist Villages initiative.  

Take a moment, breathe the history, and explore the site.

Les sentiers d’aventure vous guident à travers des paysages variés : le sentier du Siq serpente entre les rochers le long du cours d’eau, le sentier du Chute offre une chute de 20 m, et le sentier du Badan donne une vue sur la mer Morte où l’oual nubien peut être observé. wadi_Rum_Français_Long.story:
Bienvenue dans la vallée de la Lune ! 

En vous approchant du sud de la Jordanie, à environ soixante‑dix kilomètres au nord d’Aqaba, vous découvrez le vaste Wadi Rum. Son paysage désertique, parsemé de dunes et de rochers rouges, rappelle la surface de la Lune, d’où son nom de vallée du Ciel. D’immenses arches naturelles, des grottes sculptées et des formations granitiques se dressent sous un ciel d’une clarté exceptionnelle. 

Ce lieu était autrefois une étape cruciale sur les routes commerciales des Nabatéens, et les gravures et dessins gravés dans la pierre témoignent de la présence humaine depuis des millénaires. Aujourd’hui, les tribus bédouines continuent d’y vivre, préservant leurs coutumes ancestrales. 

Classé au patrimoine mondial de l’UNESCO depuis 2011, Wadi Rum attire les amateurs d’aventure, de camping, d’escalade et de safaris en 4×4. Son décor spectaculaire a servi de décor à de nombreux films internationaux, et les soirées sous les étoiles offrent une expérience inoubliable. 

Continuez votre exploration, le désert vous attend.
